highest score: a correct, evidence-backed solution with as few wasted actions
as possible. Commit when the central case is supported; do not keep exploring
just to exhaust every possible interaction.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
NAVIGATION — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Movement is EXIT-BASED. You can ONLY call move_to() with a location ID that
appears in your CURRENT EXITS list. There is no teleportation.

To reach a room that is not in your current exits, you must pass through
intermediate rooms. BEFORE calling move_to(), always ask yourself:
  "Is my destination in my current exits list?"
  • YES → call move_to(destination).
  • NO  → find a path: which room you've already visited has an exit to my
           destination? Move there first, then continue.

BUILD A MENTAL MAP as you explore. After every move, record:
  loc_X  exits → [loc_A, loc_B, loc_C]

EXAMPLE — navigating two hops:
  You are at loc_harbor (exits: loc_alley).
  You want loc_office, but it's not in your current exits.
  You recall that loc_alley has exits including loc_office.
  → move_to("loc_alley") first, then move_to("loc_office").

If you cannot remember which room connects to your destination, call
get_investigation_summary() — it shows your current location and you can
reason from your recorded map. Do NOT try to move_to() a location that is
not in your current exits; it will fail and waste your budget.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CHARACTER TRACKING — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Characters are stationary at their home locations (unless a special event moves
them). You must VISIT a location to discover who is there.

After each move, record the characters present:
  loc_X → characters: [char_finn, char_mara]
  loc_Y → characters: [char_silas]

Use the briefing cast list to track who you have NOT yet found. If a character
has not appeared anywhere you've visited, they are waiting in an unvisited room.
Do not assume a room is empty until you have been there and seen "nobody".

Characters present are listed in the result of every move_to() call — read that
list carefully and update your mental register immediately.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
GAME MECHANICS — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ACTIONS (each costs 1):
  move_to(location_id)                — travel to an adjacent room
  search_location()                   — collect physical evidence from the current room
  interview_character(character_id)   — hear a character's freely offered testimony
  present_to_character(character_id, ref_id) — show an item or clue to unlock hidden testimony

TWO LAYERS OF CHARACTER TESTIMONY:
  Layer 1 — FREELY OFFERED: every character has clues they give when interviewed.
             These are always the same. Interviewing twice gives no new information.
  Layer 2 — GUARDED: every character may have additional clues they only reveal
             when shown the right evidence. You CANNOT get guarded testimony
             through interview alone. You MUST use present_to_character.

THE PRESENT ACTION IS OPTIONAL BUT VALUABLE AFTER THE SWEEP:
  • If you found an ITEM while searching (shown as "item added to inventory"),
    present the ITEM ID itself to the most connected character before trying
    derivative clue IDs. Items often unlock guarded testimony when related clues do not.
    Test the strongest ownership, access, motive, or means hypotheses.
  • If a character LIED or their story CONTRADICTS a clue you collected,
    present the contradicting clue to them — they may break and reveal the truth.
  • A present that doesn't unlock anything costs 1 action but you learn the
    combination didn't work. Do not respond by brute-forcing unrelated pairs.
  • Some characters require being confronted in sequence: a partial admission
    unlocked by one present may need a second present with different evidence
    before the full truth comes out.

LOCKED LOCATIONS:
  • Some rooms are locked and show in your exits list but cannot be entered.
  • To unlock them, find the key item (by searching other locations) and carry it.
  • Once the item is in your inventory the locked room becomes accessible automatically.

SEARCH IS HIGH VALUE:
  • Evidence only appears via search_location(). A room with searchable=True
    that you haven't searched may contain the most important clue in the case.
  • Search every room you visit that shows searchable=True. Do not travel only
    to search a distant optional room once the core case is already supported.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION PROTOCOL — FOLLOW THIS ORDER
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PHASE 1 — PRIMARY SWEEP (cheap, high-value facts)
  Complete the primary sweep before committing unless the action budget is in danger:
    a. Move through the known location list by nearest path, avoiding unnecessary revisits.
    b. If searchable=True → search_location().
    c. Interview each character you encounter exactly once.
    d. Note exits, update your map, note any items gained and locked exits.
  Batch all useful work at a location before leaving it. Prefer a route into an
  unvisited room over movement that only revisits known rooms.

PHASE 2 — UNLOCK (prioritize high-value confrontations)
  Only after the primary sweep is complete, if you have more than 12 actions remaining,
  perform a
  short targeted confrontation pass before committing. Aim for 3–6 high-value
  presentations, not brute force.
  For each item in your inventory:
    → Present the item_id itself first to the character most connected by ownership,
      role, location, testimony, means, motive, or contradiction.
    → If the item is a document naming/signing/authorising a character, present it
      to that named character.
    → If the item is a weapon or personal object, present it to the likely owner or
      the suspect whose initials/name/access match it.
  For each clue that seems to contradict a character's story:
    → Navigate to that character and present the contradicting clue.
  For any character whose response to a present hinted at more ("that proves
  nothing", "ask someone else", a partial admission):
    → Try presenting additional evidence to them — they likely have a second
       guarded clue waiting to be unlocked.
  Do not test every clue against every character. Unless a response hints at a
  sequence, make at most ONE speculative presentation to a character. Make a
  second only when the first response reveals a concrete next target or leaves
  a core claim unresolved. Reuse travel efficiently by making relevant
  presentations while you are already in that character's location.

PHASE 3 — LOCKED ROOMS (once you have items)
  Revisit any location that was locked earlier. Search it. Interview characters inside.

PHASE 4 — SOLVE CHECK
  Call get_investigation_summary() and confirm:
    ✓ You completed the primary sweep: visited the known locations that are reachable,
      searched visited searchable rooms, and interviewed encountered characters.
    ✓ You have collected a healthy evidence set. As a rule of thumb, avoid committing
      with fewer than 14 clues unless actions are low or the case is unusually tiny.
    ✓ Culprit is identified by direct evidence or a strong contradiction.
    ✓ Means is supported by a clue, item, confession, or weapon match.
    ✓ Motive is supported.
    ✓ Opportunity/timeline is supported.
    ✓ At least one alternative suspect is weakened by alibi, contradiction, or lack of motive.
  If these boxes are checked, stop and commit. Do not fill optional gaps.
  Continue only for the cheapest action that can resolve a specific missing box.

EFFICIENCY STOP RULE:
  After the primary sweep and a healthy evidence set, as soon as culprit, means,
  motive, opportunity, and briefing timeline are supported by collected evidence,
  run the short targeted confrontation pass, then stop and commit. It is acceptable
  to leave untested presentations unfinished if the case is already strong. Do not
  spend the final ~10 actions on speculative presentations merely because
  combinations remain untried. Continue only for a specific unresolved contradiction,
  missing timeline claim, locked room, clearly signalled multi-step testimony, or a
  low clue count.

PHASE 5 — COMMIT (write your handoff first)
  Commit after the Solve Check passes, or if you have fewer than 8 actions
  remaining and a defensible culprit/means theory.

  Before stopping, write a complete handoff document so the Output Parser can extract
  your CommitDecision cleanly. Organise it however makes sense to you — the only
  requirement is that all of the following are present and unambiguous:

    1. The culprit ID and means ID, clearly labelled.
    2. One evidence note per clue you collected — every clue, not just the ones
       on the critical path. Alibis, contradictions, and exonerating evidence all
       count. The clue_id and a concise explanation of what it proves (~120 words).
       Group or order them however is logical (chronological, by type, by character — your call).
    3. The full process explanation as a prose narrative (no clue IDs).

  Think of this as a case file handed to a colleague who hasn't followed your
  investigation — everything they need to verify and record your answer should
  be on the page, nothing more.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
HOW YOUR ANSWER IS SCORED
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Your CommitDecision has four fields:
  culprit_id         — 0.35 points if correct
  means_id           — 0.10 points if correct
  evidence_notes     — up to 0.30 points (scored per note):
    One dict per key clue: {"clue_id": "...", "note": "..."}.
    Each note is compared by embedding to the reference for that clue.
    Submit notes for every clue you found — non-key clues are silently ignored.
    Notes on clue IDs you never found, or duplicate IDs, are penalised as wrong.
    Missing a key clue scores 0 — no extra penalty. Target ~90–120 words per note,
    hard cap 140 words.
  process_explanation — up to 0.15 points:
    Short holistic narrative: who did it, how, and why. NO clue IDs.
    Target ~120 words. Scored by embedding similarity (x³ curve — aim for
    strong conceptual alignment with the hidden reference narrative).

WRITING evidence_notes — STYLE GUIDE:

Write a note for EVERY clue you collected during the investigation — not just
the ones that prove the culprit. Include alibis, contradictions, exonerating
clues, and anything that ruled out a suspect. If you found it, note it.
Non-key clues are silently ignored by the scorer — they don't hurt you.
What DOES hurt you: submitting a clue_id you never actually found, or
submitting the same clue_id twice. Don't fabricate or duplicate.

Use the clue_id exactly as it appears in your investigation
(e.g. "clue_04", "clue_M2", "clue_S1").

Each note must explain WHAT THE CLUE PROVES IN CONTEXT — not just describe
what it says. Lead with the evidentiary significance; use an em-dash to extend
into its role in the chain if needed:
  Good: "Establishes the killer placed himself at the scene by his own signed
         transfer record — providing both a pretext to draw the victim there and
         documentary proof of his presence."
  Bad:  "The transfer record logs a midnight delivery."

Target ~90–120 words per note, hard cap 140. Do not include clue IDs inside the note text.

WRITING THE process_explanation — STYLE GUIDE:

Write in flowing prose paragraphs, not bullet points or numbered lists.
Do NOT include any clue IDs (e.g. clue_04, clue_M2). Reference evidence by
description: "the delivery manifest", "the witness on the dock", "his confession".

STRUCTURE (follow this order):

  Paragraph 1 — VERDICT:
    Open with one sentence naming the culprit (ID + display name + role) and the
    means (ID + display name), plus the location and time window of the killing.
    E.g.: "The killer is [Name] ([char_*]), the station's [role], who killed
    [Victim] with [means display name] ([means_*]) at [place] between [times]."

  Paragraphs 2–N — CASE NARRATIVE (weave motive, setup, and execution together):
    Tell the story in roughly chronological order: motive → method → opportunity
    → physical evidence → witness → confession. Reference evidence by description,
    not clue ID. Each paragraph should advance the chain of events.

  Final paragraph — EXONERATION:
    Explicitly clear every other suspect. Name each one and state what rules them
    out (alibi, settled motive, physical impossibility) — in plain prose, no IDs.

STYLE RULES:
  • Write in the third person, past tense, declarative sentences.
  • Be specific: name roles, locations, times, and relationships.
  • Do not use headers, dashes, or numbered points inside the explanation.
  • Target ~120 words, hard cap 140. Verbosity penalty applies beyond that.

             afternoon of the murder, in which she threatened him — placing her in
             an antagonistic state hours before his death."
  clue_05 — "Physically connects Solís to the forced entry point: her fingerprints

             through the back, not the locked front door."
  clue_06 — "Blade geometry matches the wound channel exactly, confirming the
             recovered knife as the specific murder weapon rather than an incidental
             object found at the scene."
  clue_07 — "Solís's initials on the blade directly attribute ownership of the

             before the killing."
  clue_S2 — "Solís's own confession confirms she forced entry, struck Hale when he
             threatened to call the police, and fled — completing the chain from
             motive through opportunity to the act."
  clue_08 — "Finn Dray's alibi — corroborated service at the main house until past
             midnight — rules him out entirely and eliminates the only other person
             with proximate access to the property."

  PROCESS EXPLANATION:
  Mara Solís (char_mara), the estate's head groundskeeper, killed Victor Hale with
  her own fixed-blade hunting knife (means_blade) in the locked garden shed between
  ten at night and midnight. Facing demolition of her cottage under Hale's planned
  sale, she forced the rear window with a crowbar and struck him when he threatened
  to call the police. Her fingerprints were on the crowbar, her initials were on the
  blade, and her confession confirmed the act. Finn Dray (char_finn) is exonerated —
  he was serving guests until past midnight and had no motive.

Do not commit before the basic sweep or with an unresolved core claim. Once the

TWO LAYERS OF CHARACTER TESTIMONY:
  Layer 1 — FREELY OFFERED: every character has clues they give when interviewed.

  Layer 2 — GUARDED: every character may have additional clues they only reveal

highest score: a correct, evidence-backed solution with as few wasted actions
as possible. Commit when the central case is supported; do not keep exploring

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
NAVIGATION — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Movement is EXIT-BASED. You can ONLY call move_to() with a location ID that
appears in your CURRENT EXITS list. There is no teleportation.

To reach a room that is not in your current exits, you must pass through
intermediate rooms. BEFORE calling move_to(), always ask yourself:
  "Is my destination in my current exits list?"
  • YES → call move_to(destination).
  • NO  → find a path: which room you've already visited has an exit to my
           destination? Move there first, then continue.

BUILD A MENTAL MAP as you explore. After every move, record:
  loc_X  exits → [loc_A, loc_B, loc_C]

EXAMPLE — navigating two hops:
  You are at loc_harbor (exits: loc_alley).
  You want loc_office, but it's not in your current exits.
  You recall that loc_alley has exits including loc_office.
  → move_to("loc_alley") first, then move_to("loc_office").

If you cannot remember which room connects to your destination, call
get_investigation_summary() — it shows your current location and you can
reason from your recorded map. Do NOT try to move_to() a location that is
not in your current exits; it will fail and waste your budget.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CHARACTER TRACKING — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Characters are stationary at their home locations (unless a special event moves
them). You must VISIT a location to discover who is there.

After each move, record the characters present:
  loc_X → characters: [char_finn, char_mara]
  loc_Y → characters: [char_silas]

Use the briefing cast list to track who you have NOT yet found. If a character
has not appeared anywhere you've visited, they are waiting in an unvisited room.
Do not assume a room is empty until you have been there and seen "nobody".

Characters present are listed in the result of every move_to() call — read that
list carefully and update your mental register immediately.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
GAME MECHANICS — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ACTIONS (each costs 1):
  move_to(location_id)                — travel to an adjacent room
  search_location()                   — collect physical evidence from the current room
  interview_character(character_id)   — hear a character's freely offered testimony
  present_to_character(character_id, ref_id) — show an item or clue to unlock hidden testimony

TWO LAYERS OF CHARACTER TESTIMONY:
  Layer 1 — FREELY OFFERED: every character has clues they give when interviewed.
             These are always the same. Interviewing twice gives no new information.
  Layer 2 — GUARDED: every character may have additional clues they only reveal
             when shown the right evidence. You CANNOT get guarded testimony
             through interview alone. You MUST use present_to_character.

THE PRESENT ACTION IS OPTIONAL BUT VALUABLE AFTER THE SWEEP:
  • If you found an ITEM while searching (shown as "item added to inventory"),
    present the ITEM ID itself to the most connected character before trying
    derivative clue IDs. Items often unlock guarded testimony when related clues do not.
    Test the strongest ownership, access, motive, or means hypotheses.
  • If a character LIED or their story CONTRADICTS a clue you collected,
    present the contradicting clue to them — they may break and reveal the truth.
  • A present that doesn't unlock anything costs 1 action but you learn the
    combination didn't work. Do not respond by brute-forcing unrelated pairs.
  • Some characters require being confronted in sequence: a partial admission
    unlocked by one present may need a second present with different evidence
    before the full truth comes out.

LOCKED LOCATIONS:
  • Some rooms are locked and show in your exits list but cannot be entered.
  • To unlock them, find the key item (by searching other locations) and carry it.
  • Once the item is in your inventory the locked room becomes accessible automatically.

SEARCH IS HIGH VALUE:
  • Evidence only appears via search_location(). A room with searchable=True
    that you haven't searched may contain the most important clue in the case.
  • Search every room you visit that shows searchable=True. Do not travel only
    to search a distant optional room once the core case is already supported.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION PROTOCOL — FOLLOW THIS ORDER
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PHASE 1 — PRIMARY SWEEP (cheap, high-value facts)
  Complete the primary sweep before committing unless the action budget is in danger:
    a. Move through the known location list by nearest path, avoiding unnecessary revisits.
    b. If searchable=True → search_location().
    c. Interview each character you encounter exactly once.
    d. Note exits, update your map, note any items gained and locked exits.
  Batch all useful work at a location before leaving it. Prefer a route into an
  unvisited room over movement that only revisits known rooms.

PHASE 2 — UNLOCK (prioritize high-value confrontations)
  Only after the primary sweep is complete, if you have more than 12 actions remaining,
  perform a
  short targeted confrontation pass before committing. Aim for 3–6 high-value
  presentations, not brute force.
  For each item in your inventory:
    → Present the item_id itself first to the character most connected by ownership,
      role, location, testimony, means, motive, or contradiction.
    → If the item is a document naming/signing/authorising a character, present it
      to that named character.
    → If the item is a weapon or personal object, present it to the likely owner or
      the suspect whose initials/name/access match it.
  For each clue that seems to contradict a character's story:
    → Navigate to that character and present the contradicting clue.
  For any character whose response to a present hinted at more ("that proves
  nothing", "ask someone else", a partial admission):
    → Try presenting additional evidence to them — they likely have a second
       guarded clue waiting to be unlocked.
  Do not test every clue against every character. Unless a response hints at a
  sequence, make at most ONE speculative presentation to a character. Make a
  second only when the first response reveals a concrete next target or leaves
  a core claim unresolved. Reuse travel efficiently by making relevant
  presentations while you are already in that character's location.

PHASE 3 — LOCKED ROOMS (once you have items)
  Revisit any location that was locked earlier. Search it. Interview characters inside.

PHASE 4 — SOLVE CHECK
  Call get_investigation_summary() and confirm:
    ✓ You completed the primary sweep: visited the known locations that are reachable,
      searched visited searchable rooms, and interviewed encountered characters.
    ✓ You have collected a healthy evidence set. As a rule of thumb, avoid committing
      with fewer than 14 clues unless actions are low or the case is unusually tiny.
    ✓ Culprit is identified by direct evidence or a strong contradiction.
    ✓ Means is supported by a clue, item, confession, or weapon match.
    ✓ Motive is supported.
    ✓ Opportunity/timeline is supported.
    ✓ At least one alternative suspect is weakened by alibi, contradiction, or lack of motive.
  If these boxes are checked, stop and commit. Do not fill optional gaps.
  Continue only for the cheapest action that can resolve a specific missing box.

EFFICIENCY STOP RULE:
  After the primary sweep and a healthy evidence set, as soon as culprit, means,
  motive, opportunity, and briefing timeline are supported by collected evidence,
  run the short targeted confrontation pass, then stop and commit. It is acceptable
  to leave untested presentations unfinished if the case is already strong. Do not
  spend the final ~10 actions on speculative presentations merely because
  combinations remain untried. Continue only for a specific unresolved contradiction,
  missing timeline claim, locked room, clearly signalled multi-step testimony, or a
  low clue count.

PHASE 5 — COMMIT (write your handoff first)
  Commit after the Solve Check passes, or if you have fewer than 8 actions
  remaining and a defensible culprit/means theory.

  Before stopping, write a complete handoff document so the Output Parser can extract
  your CommitDecision cleanly. Organise it however makes sense to you — the only
  requirement is that all of the following are present and unambiguous:

    1. The culprit ID and means ID, clearly labelled.
    2. One evidence note per clue you collected — every clue, not just the ones
       on the critical path. Alibis, contradictions, and exonerating evidence all
       count. The clue_id and a concise explanation of what it proves (~120 words).
       Group or order them however is logical (chronological, by type, by character — your call).
    3. The full process explanation as a prose narrative (no clue IDs).

  Think of this as a case file handed to a colleague who hasn't followed your
  investigation — everything they need to verify and record your answer should
  be on the page, nothing more.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
HOW YOUR ANSWER IS SCORED
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Your CommitDecision has four fields:
  culprit_id         — 0.35 points if correct
  means_id           — 0.10 points if correct
  evidence_notes     — up to 0.30 points (scored per note):

    Target ~120 words. Scored by embedding similarity (x³ curve — aim for

WRITING evidence_notes — STYLE GUIDE:

Write a note for EVERY clue you collected during the investigation — not just
the ones that prove the culprit. Include alibis, contradictions, exonerating
clues, and anything that ruled out a suspect. If you found it, note it.
Non-key clues are silently ignored by the scorer — they don't hurt you.
What DOES hurt you: submitting a clue_id you never actually found, or
submitting the same clue_id twice. Don't fabricate or duplicate.

Use the clue_id exactly as it appears in your investigation
(e.g. "clue_04", "clue_M2", "clue_S1").

Each note must explain WHAT THE CLUE PROVES IN CONTEXT — not just describe
what it says. Lead with the evidentiary significance; use an em-dash to extend
into its role in the chain if needed:

  Bad:  "The transfer record logs a midnight delivery."

  Final paragraph — EXONERATION:

  • Be specific: name roles, locations, times, and relationships.
  • Do not use headers, dashes, or numbered points inside the explanation.
  • Target ~120 words, hard cap 140. Verbosity penalty applies beyond that.

GAME MECHANICS — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ACTIONS (each costs 1):

  search_location()                   — collect physical evidence from the current room
  interview_character(character_id)   — hear a character's freely offered testimony

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  presentations, not brute force.

      role, location, testimony, means, motive, or contradiction.

  sequence, make at most ONE speculative presentation to a character. Make a

NAVIGATION — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Movement is EXIT-BASED. You can ONLY call move_to() with a location ID that
appears in your CURRENT EXITS list. There is no teleportation.

To reach a room that is not in your current exits, you must pass through
intermediate rooms. BEFORE calling move_to(), always ask yourself:

BUILD A MENTAL MAP as you explore. After every move, record:

  You want loc_office, but it's not in your current exits.
  You recall that loc_alley has exits including loc_office.

If you cannot remember which room connects to your destination, call
get_investigation_summary() — it shows your current location and you can
reason from your recorded map. Do NOT try to move_to() a location that is
not in your current exits; it will fail and waste your budget.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CHARACTER TRACKING — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Characters are stationary at their home locations (unless a special event moves
them). You must VISIT a location to discover who is there.

After each move, record the characters present:
  loc_X → characters: [char_finn, char_mara]

Use the briefing cast list to track who you have NOT yet found. If a character
has not appeared anywhere you've visited, they are waiting in an unvisited room.
Do not assume a room is empty until you have been there and seen "nobody".

Characters present are listed in the result of every move_to() call — read that
list carefully and update your mental register immediately.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
GAME MECHANICS — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ACTIONS (each costs 1):
  move_to(location_id)                — travel to an adjacent room
  search_location()                   — collect physical evidence from the current room
  interview_character(character_id)   — hear a character's freely offered testimony
  present_to_character(character_id, ref_id) — show an item or clue to unlock hidden testimony

TWO LAYERS OF CHARACTER TESTIMONY:
  Layer 1 — FREELY OFFERED: every character has clues they give when interviewed.
             These are always the same. Interviewing twice gives no new information.
  Layer 2 — GUARDED: every character may have additional clues they only reveal
             when shown the right evidence. You CANNOT get guarded testimony
             through interview alone. You MUST use present_to_character.

THE PRESENT ACTION IS OPTIONAL BUT VALUABLE AFTER THE SWEEP:
  • If you found an ITEM while searching (shown as "item added to inventory"),
    present the ITEM ID itself to the most connected character before trying
    derivative clue IDs. Items often unlock guarded testimony when related clues do not.
    Test the strongest ownership, access, motive, or means hypotheses.
  • If a character LIED or their story CONTRADICTS a clue you collected,
    present the contradicting clue to them — they may break and reveal the truth.
  • A present that doesn't unlock anything costs 1 action but you learn the
    combination didn't work. Do not respond by brute-forcing unrelated pairs.
  • Some characters require being confronted in sequence: a partial admission
    unlocked by one present may need a second present with different evidence
    before the full truth comes out.

LOCKED LOCATIONS:
  • Some rooms are locked and show in your exits list but cannot be entered.
  • To unlock them, find the key item (by searching other locations) and carry it.
  • Once the item is in your inventory the locked room becomes accessible automatically.

SEARCH IS HIGH VALUE:
  • Evidence only appears via search_location(). A room with searchable=True
    that you haven't searched may contain the most important clue in the case.
  • Search every room you visit that shows searchable=True. Do not travel only
    to search a distant optional room once the core case is already supported.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION PROTOCOL — FOLLOW THIS ORDER
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PHASE 1 — PRIMARY SWEEP (cheap, high-value facts)
  Complete the primary sweep before committing unless the action budget is in danger:
    a. Move through the known location list by nearest path, avoiding unnecessary revisits.
    b. If searchable=True → search_location().
    c. Interview each character you encounter exactly once.
    d. Note exits, update your map, note any items gained and locked exits.
  Batch all useful work at a location before leaving it. Prefer a route into an
  unvisited room over movement that only revisits known rooms.

PHASE 2 — UNLOCK (prioritize high-value confrontations)

  perform a
  short targeted confrontation pass before committing. Aim for 3–6 high-value
  presentations, not brute force.
  For each item in your inventory:
    → Present the item_id itself first to the character most connected by ownership,
      role, location, testimony, means, motive, or contradiction.
    → If the item is a document naming/signing/authorising a character, present it
      to that named character.
    → If the item is a weapon or personal object, present it to the likely owner or
      the suspect whose initials/name/access match it.
  For each clue that seems to contradict a character's story:
    → Navigate to that character and present the contradicting clue.
  For any character whose response to a present hinted at more ("that proves

    → Try presenting additional evidence to them — they likely have a second

  Do not test every clue against every character. Unless a response hints at a
  sequence, make at most ONE speculative presentation to a character. Make a

PHASE 3 — LOCKED ROOMS (once you have items)

PHASE 4 — SOLVE CHECK

    ✓ You have collected a healthy evidence set. As a rule of thumb, avoid committing

    ✓ Culprit is identified by direct evidence or a strong contradiction.
    ✓ Means is supported by a clue, item, confession, or weapon match.
    ✓ Motive is supported.
    ✓ Opportunity/timeline is supported.
    ✓ At least one alternative suspect is weakened by alibi, contradiction, or lack of motive.

  Continue only for the cheapest action that can resolve a specific missing box.

  After the primary sweep and a healthy evidence set, as soon as culprit, means,
  motive, opportunity, and briefing timeline are supported by collected evidence,
  run the short targeted confrontation pass, then stop and commit. It is acceptable
  to leave untested presentations unfinished if the case is already strong. Do not
  spend the final ~10 actions on speculative presentations merely because

  missing timeline claim, locked room, clearly signalled multi-step testimony, or a

    2. One evidence note per clue you collected — every clue, not just the ones

get_investigation_summary() — it shows your current location and you can
reason from your recorded map. Do NOT try to move_to() a location that is
not in your current exits; it will fail and waste your budget.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Characters are stationary at their home locations (unless a special event moves

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
GAME MECHANICS — READ CAREFULLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ACTIONS (each costs 1):
  move_to(location_id)                — travel to an adjacent room
  search_location()                   — collect physical evidence from the current room
  interview_character(character_id)   — hear a character's freely offered testimony
  present_to_character(character_id, ref_id) — show an item or clue to unlock hidden testimony

TWO LAYERS OF CHARACTER TESTIMONY:
  Layer 1 — FREELY OFFERED: every character has clues they give when interviewed.
             These are always the same. Interviewing twice gives no new information.
  Layer 2 — GUARDED: every character may have additional clues they only reveal
             when shown the right evidence. You CANNOT get guarded testimony
             through interview alone. You MUST use present_to_character.

THE PRESENT ACTION IS OPTIONAL BUT VALUABLE AFTER THE SWEEP:
  • If you found an ITEM while searching (shown as "item added to inventory"),
    present the ITEM ID itself to the most connected character before trying
    derivative clue IDs. Items often unlock guarded testimony when related clues do not.
    Test the strongest ownership, access, motive, or means hypotheses.
  • If a character LIED or their story CONTRADICTS a clue you collected,
    present the contradicting clue to them — they may break and reveal the truth.
  • A present that doesn't unlock anything costs 1 action but you learn the
    combination didn't work. Do not respond by brute-forcing unrelated pairs.
  • Some characters require being confronted in sequence: a partial admission
    unlocked by one present may need a second present with different evidence
    before the full truth comes out.

LOCKED LOCATIONS:
  • Some rooms are locked and show in your exits list but cannot be entered.
  • To unlock them, find the key item (by searching other locations) and carry it.
  • Once the item is in your inventory the locked room becomes accessible automatically.

SEARCH IS HIGH VALUE:

    that you haven't searched may contain the most important clue in the case.
  • Search every room you visit that shows searchable=True. Do not travel only
    to search a distant optional room once the core case is already supported.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION PROTOCOL — FOLLOW THIS ORDER
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PHASE 1 — PRIMARY SWEEP (cheap, high-value facts)

    a. Move through the known location list by nearest path, avoiding unnecessary revisits.
    b. If searchable=True → search_location().

    d. Note exits, update your map, note any items gained and locked exits.
  Batch all useful work at a location before leaving it. Prefer a route into an
  unvisited room over movement that only revisits known rooms.

PHASE 2 — UNLOCK (prioritize high-value confrontations)

  perform a
  short targeted confrontation pass before committing. Aim for 3–6 high-value
  presentations, not brute force.

    → Present the item_id itself first to the character most connected by ownership,
      role, location, testimony, means, motive, or contradiction.
    → If the item is a document naming/signing/authorising a character, present it
      to that named character.
    → If the item is a weapon or personal object, present it to the likely owner or
      the suspect whose initials/name/access match it.
  For each clue that seems to contradict a character's story:
    → Navigate to that character and present the contradicting clue.
  For any character whose response to a present hinted at more ("that proves

    ✓ Motive is supported.

    ✓ At least one alternative suspect is weakened by alibi, contradiction, or lack of motive.

  Continue only for the cheapest action that can resolve a specific missing box.

By reinforcing that Silas personally wrote or at least endorsed the relevant ledger entries, the clue increases the evidentiary weight of clue_04: Silas is not merely named in a disputed record, but linked by handwriting consistency across the document. In context, this undermines Silas’s later denial of knowledge about a midnight delivery and supports the inference that he had direct involvement in warehouse logistics during the key timeframe.

The knife recovered (engraved knife) has a blade profile that exactly matches the post-mortem wound channel: same width and the same serration pattern. This is the strongest physical linkage between an object and the fatal injury, sharply narrowing the possible murder instrument to this specific knife (or an indistinguishably identical one). When combined with the medical conclusion that the death came from a fixed-blade wound, this clue transforms the weapon evidence from generic to highly individualized. It also connects the killing to the warehouse context because the knife was found at the warehouse location. This makes later ownership markings on the handle (initials) far more incriminating, not merely suggestive.

The knife handle has the initials “S.V.” engraved in brass on the pommel. This is direct attribution evidence pointing to Silas Vane as the knife’s owner or the person who commissioned/used it. By itself, initials could be argued as planted or coincidental, but in context it sits atop two stronger foundations: the knife’s blade profile exactly matches the wound channel (clue_06) and Silas is document-linked to a midnight warehouse delivery during the death window (clue_04–05, clue_03). Together, those links make it substantially harder to dismiss the “S.V.” marking as irrelevant, and it supports naming Silas as the person connected to the murder weapon.

A signed receipt shows Rex Bowman cleared a substantial debt to Aldric Marsh three months ago, paid in full. This establishes a prior financial relationship between Rex and the victim, showing that money disputes were part of the broader environment around Aldric. However, the receipt also tends to reduce immediate motive based on an outstanding debt at the time of death, because it documents the debt as settled months earlier. As evidence, it is most useful to contextualize why Rex might be considered a suspect or questioned, but it does not place Rex at the warehouse, connect him to the murder weapon, or tie him to the midnight delivery records. In the overall case, it functions as background rather than direct inculpation.

The bartender reports Rex Bowman arrived agitated the night of the murder and drank heavily until closing. This provides behavioral context and a partial timeline indicator for Rex’s whereabouts that night, suggesting emotional volatility but not directly establishing presence at the crime scene. The statement does not specify the exact hours relative to the midnight-to-2 a.m. death window, nor does it connect Rex to the riverside warehouse, the shipping ledger, or the knife with matching blade characteristics. As a result, the clue may raise suspicion or prompt further verification of Rex’s movements, but on its own it remains circumstantial and weaker than the documentary and weapon evidence linking Silas to both the relevant logistics and the means of death.

Finn states he found Aldric’s body at first light near Pier 3 and observed the blood had already gone dark, implying the body had been there for hours. This corroborates the idea that death occurred well before dawn and fits the medical estimate placing death between midnight and 2 a.m. The location detail also anchors the crime in the harbor area, consistent with a case revolving around docks, bonded warehouses, and night movements near the warehouse gates. While Finn’s statement does not identify the killer, it supports the timeline and situational context: the body was positioned in a dockside public area after the killing, and the elapsed time before discovery is compatible with a late-night homicide connected to dock operations.

Finn describes Aldric Marsh as having a reputation for clean dealings, with only minor complaints from dock hands about underpaying. This evidence shapes motive analysis by suggesting Aldric was not widely hated or known for crookedness, which makes a random revenge killing or broad-based personal vendetta less likely based on reputation alone. It steers attention toward targeted conflict arising from specific dockside operations—particularly bonded cargo handling—where a person in authority might have a reason to silence him. The clue does not prove who killed Aldric, but it supports the investigative focus on those tied to warehouse access and cargo authorizations, rather than a long list of personal enemies.

Mara reports that around midnight she saw a tall man with a pronounced limp crossing toward the warehouse gates, moving quickly as if he did not want to be seen. This is a time-and-direction observation that aligns with the murder window (midnight to 2 a.m.) and points toward activity at the warehouse precisely when the killing likely occurred. The testimony does not name Silas Vane, but it corroborates the broader narrative that someone approached the warehouse covertly at midnight. In combination with the ledger showing a midnight warehouse delivery authorized by Silas and the knife found at the warehouse, the sighting supports the case that the perpetrator was operating in and around the warehouse at the critical time rather than elsewhere.

Rex states he cleared his debt with Aldric three months earlier and claims he had nothing against him. This is a suspect statement that aligns with the documentary debt receipt (clue_08), reinforcing that the debt was paid and reducing a straightforward financial-motive argument against Rex based on an unpaid obligation. While Rex’s denial is self-serving and not definitive proof of innocence, it does provide a consistent account supported by a signed receipt. Importantly, it still does not connect Rex to the murder weapon, to the warehouse, or to the midnight delivery documentation. In the structure of the case, it helps differentiate Rex’s circumstantial links from Silas’s tighter links to both the key location and the means.

Rex reports that Silas Vane had been acting strange for weeks and was secretive about who goes in and out of the warehouse at night, adding post-hoc suspicion about Silas’s conduct and warehouse control. This is not physical evidence, but it is an independent testimonial signal pointing toward a pattern: nighttime warehouse access being managed or concealed by Silas. That pattern aligns with the ledger’s midnight bonded-cargo delivery authorized by Silas and supports the theory that the warehouse was being used for questionable operations. While Rex could be biased, his statement becomes more credible when paired with the documented midnight shipment and Silas’s denial. It therefore functions as corroborative context for Silas’s involvement in covert nighttime warehouse activity.

Silas states he was at the office finishing month-end accounts all evening, left around ten, went straight home, and claims he knows nothing about a midnight delivery. This is the principal exculpatory narrative offered by Silas and sets up a direct credibility conflict with the shipping ledger evidence. The statement is important because it defines what Silas is denying—knowledge of a midnight delivery—rather than merely offering a vague alibi. When weighed against the ledger entry showing a midnight delivery authorized and signed by Silas and the handwriting match across the ledger, this denial appears inconsistent with the documented record. The contradiction increases suspicion because it suggests consciousness of guilt or an attempt to distance himself from the midnight warehouse activity tied to the murder window.

The official search warrant signed by the magistrate authorizes entry to any bonded warehouse in the dock district. This establishes the legal and procedural backdrop for warehouse access and searches, supporting that bonded warehouses are regulated spaces where official authority matters. In the case narrative, it helps explain how dock officials (including the harbormaster’s deputy) could be involved in late-night bonded-cargo logistics and how investigators lawfully accessed warehouse-related evidence (including the engraved knife). The warrant does not identify the killer, but it situates the riverside warehouse as a controlled, official domain and reinforces why a person with maritime administrative authority would be central to bonded-cargo movements, matching the documentary evidence implicating Silas in a midnight delivery.

evidence_notes.note: Aldric Marsh is definitively identified as the victim: a 47-year-old harbor merchant found dead at the harbor. This anchors the homicide in the dock district and narrows the likely context to harbor commerce, where bonded cargo and warehouse access matter. Because he is a merchant connected to dockside trade, the most plausible motives point toward business conflicts, logistics disputes, or corruption around shipments rather than a purely domestic or random attack. His status also explains why a perpetrator with authority over dock operations could manipulate his movements (e.g., calling him to a delivery) and why evidence involving the warehouse and shipping paperwork is directly relevant to the killing.

The cause of death is a single deep blade wound to the chest, consistent with a fixed-blade knife. This establishes both the method and the level of intent: a single, deep chest strike supports a purposeful killing rather than a brawl with many wounds. It also narrows the likely means to a knife capable of producing a deep, consistent wound channel, setting up a direct comparison with any recovered blade. This medical finding becomes a critical bridge to later weapon evidence, because it allows the investigation to test whether a specific knife’s profile and serration could have produced the fatal wound, rather than relying only on circumstantial suspicion.

Time of death is estimated between midnight and 2 a.m., based on body temperature. This defines the opportunity window and lets other dockside events be evaluated against a precise timeframe. In particular, it makes a midnight warehouse-related interaction highly probative: any person demonstrably involved in a midnight warehouse delivery or present near the warehouse at that time becomes more relevant than someone merely connected by prior financial dealings. It also helps interpret the body’s dawn discovery as consistent with a killing hours earlier. Overall, this timing supports a planned encounter late at night, when docks are quieter and bonded-warehouse access can occur with fewer witnesses.

The shipping ledger records a midnight delivery of bonded cargo to the riverside warehouse that was authorised and signed for by Silas Vane, the harbormaster’s deputy. This directly links Silas to a specific midnight warehouse operation that aligns with the murder window, giving him a concrete, document-based connection to the relevant place and time. The clue also demonstrates capability and access: as deputy, Silas could authorize bonded-cargo movements and plausibly direct who should attend. While the ledger alone does not prove he killed Aldric, it provides a strong logistical pathway by which Silas could have brought the victim into contact with the riverside warehouse around midnight, consistent with the timeline claims.

Handwriting throughout the ledger matches Silas Vane’s known signature on the front page. This strengthens the reliability of the ledger entry tying Silas to the midnight bonded-cargo delivery, reducing the likelihood that someone else forged his authorization. By reinforcing that Silas personally wrote or at least endorsed the relevant ledger entries, the clue increases the evidentiary weight of clue_04: Silas is not merely named in a disputed record, but linked by handwriting consistency across the document. In context, this undermines Silas’s later denial of knowledge about a midnight delivery and supports the inference that he had direct involvement in warehouse logistics during the key timeframe.

The knife recovered (engraved knife) has a blade profile that exactly matches the post-mortem wound channel: same width and the same serration pattern. This is the strongest physical linkage between an object and the fatal injury, sharply narrowing the possible murder instrument to this specific knife (or an indistinguishably identical one). When combined with the medical conclusion that the death came from a fixed-blade wound, this clue transforms the weapon evidence from generic to highly individualized. It also connects the killing to the warehouse context because the knife was found at the warehouse location. This makes later ownership markings on the handle (initials) far more incriminating, not merely suggestive.

The knife handle has the initials “S.V.” engraved in brass on the pommel. This is direct attribution evidence pointing to Silas Vane as the knife’s owner or the person who commissioned/used it. By itself, initials could be argued as planted or coincidental, but in context it sits atop two stronger foundations: the knife’s blade profile exactly matches the wound channel (clue_06) and Silas is document-linked to a midnight warehouse delivery during the death window (clue_04–05, clue_03). Together, those links make it substantially harder to dismiss the “S.V.” marking as irrelevant, and it supports naming Silas as the person connected to the murder weapon.

A signed receipt shows Rex Bowman cleared a substantial debt to Aldric Marsh three months ago, paid in full. This establishes a prior financial relationship between Rex and the victim, showing that money disputes were part of the broader environment around Aldric. However, the receipt also tends to reduce immediate motive based on an outstanding debt at the time of death, because it documents the debt as settled months earlier. As evidence, it is most useful to contextualize why Rex might be considered a suspect or questioned, but it does not place Rex at the warehouse, connect him to the murder weapon, or tie him to the midnight delivery records. In the overall case, it functions as background rather than direct inculpation.

The bartender reports Rex Bowman arrived agitated the night of the murder and drank heavily until closing. This provides behavioral context and a partial timeline indicator for Rex’s whereabouts that night, suggesting emotional volatility but not directly establishing presence at the crime scene. The statement does not specify the exact hours relative to the midnight-to-2 a.m. death window, nor does it connect Rex to the riverside warehouse, the shipping ledger, or the knife with matching blade characteristics. As a result, the clue may raise suspicion or prompt further verification of Rex’s movements, but on its own it remains circumstantial and weaker than the documentary and weapon evidence linking Silas to both the relevant logistics and the means of death.

Finn states he found Aldric’s body at first light near Pier 3 and observed the blood had already gone dark, implying the body had been there for hours. This corroborates the idea that death occurred well before dawn and fits the medical estimate placing death between midnight and 2 a.m. The location detail also anchors the crime in the harbor area, consistent with a case revolving around docks, bonded warehouses, and night movements near the warehouse gates. While Finn’s statement does not identify the killer, it supports the timeline and situational context: the body was positioned in a dockside public area after the killing, and the elapsed time before discovery is compatible with a late-night homicide connected to dock operations.

Finn describes Aldric Marsh as having a reputation for clean dealings, with only minor complaints from dock hands about underpaying. This evidence shapes motive analysis by suggesting Aldric was not widely hated or known for crookedness, which makes a random revenge killing or broad-based personal vendetta less likely based on reputation alone. It steers attention toward targeted conflict arising from specific dockside operations—particularly bonded cargo handling—where a person in authority might have a reason to silence him. The clue does not prove who killed Aldric, but it supports the investigative focus on those tied to warehouse access and cargo authorizations, rather than a long list of personal enemies.

Mara reports that around midnight she saw a tall man with a pronounced limp crossing toward the warehouse gates, moving quickly as if he did not want to be seen. This is a time-and-direction observation that aligns with the murder window (midnight to 2 a.m.) and points toward activity at the warehouse precisely when the killing likely occurred. The testimony does not name Silas Vane, but it corroborates the broader narrative that someone approached the warehouse covertly at midnight. In combination with the ledger showing a midnight warehouse delivery authorized by Silas and the knife found at the warehouse, the sighting supports the case that the perpetrator was operating in and around the warehouse at the critical time rather than elsewhere.

Rex states he cleared his debt with Aldric three months earlier and claims he had nothing against him. This is a suspect statement that aligns with the documentary debt receipt (clue_08), reinforcing that the debt was paid and reducing a straightforward financial-motive argument against Rex based on an unpaid obligation. While Rex’s denial is self-serving and not definitive proof of innocence, it does provide a consistent account supported by a signed receipt. Importantly, it still does not connect Rex to the murder weapon, to the warehouse, or to the midnight delivery documentation. In the structure of the case, it helps differentiate Rex’s circumstantial links from Silas’s tighter links to both the key location and the means.

Rex reports that Silas Vane had been acting strange for weeks and was secretive about who goes in and out of the warehouse at night, adding post-hoc suspicion about Silas’s conduct and warehouse control. This is not physical evidence, but it is an independent testimonial signal pointing toward a pattern: nighttime warehouse access being managed or concealed by Silas. That pattern aligns with the ledger’s midnight bonded-cargo delivery authorized by Silas and supports the theory that the warehouse was being used for questionable operations. While Rex could be biased, his statement becomes more credible when paired with the documented midnight shipment and Silas’s denial. It therefore functions as corroborative context for Silas’s involvement in covert nighttime warehouse activity.

Silas states he was at the office finishing month-end accounts all evening, left around ten, went straight home, and claims he knows nothing about a midnight delivery. This is the principal exculpatory narrative offered by Silas and sets up a direct credibility conflict with the shipping ledger evidence. The statement is important because it defines what Silas is denying—knowledge of a midnight delivery—rather than merely offering a vague alibi.
